passage:
"The seller wants forty thousand for the second-hand scooter," Elizabeth said, reading the message aloud. "You could offer thirty-five and feel great."
Aparna shook her head. "Wait. If I'd never heard forty, what would I think it's worth?"
"No idea. That's why he gave a number."
"Exactly. So let's find out without his number." She opened her laptop. "Same model, same year. Let's find three others."
They scrolled. One listing said twenty-eight. A mechanic friend, on the phone, said twenty-five to thirty for that condition. Another listing was thirty-one.
"So thirty-five isn't a great deal," Elizabeth said slowly.
"It's just a smaller version of his number." Aparna closed the laptop. "I'll offer twenty-eight and explain why. If he says no, there are others."
Elizabeth laughed. "You'd have paid thirty-five yesterday."
"Yesterday I only had his number."

qa.q: What price did the seller first ask for the scooter?
qa.a: The seller asked forty thousand.

qa.q: Why does Aparna refuse to start from the seller's forty?
qa.a: She feels wary of letting his number set her sense of value, so she wants to judge the scooter as if she had never heard it.

qa.q: What steps did Aparna take before deciding, and why do they work?
qa.a: She asked what she would think without the first figure and gathered three independent comparisons, a mechanic's view and two listings, so her offer rests on evidence.

qa.q: How does Elizabeth's view of thirty-five change during the conversation?
qa.a: Elizabeth first sees thirty-five as a good offer, then realises it is only a smaller version of the seller's number.

grounding: It shows a decider asking what she would judge without the first figure and gathering independent comparisons before making an offer.

passage:
Last Diwali, my cousin told us a story about a dog in his colony that bit a boy on the leg. He showed us the scar on the boy's photo. I'm Pankaj, and I was nine, and I couldn't stop thinking about it.
After that, every dog looked dangerous. The old brown dog that sleeps outside our building, who never even barks, suddenly seemed like a wolf. I crossed the road whenever I saw him. When my friend Dilnaz stroked him, I shouted at her to stop.
"He's been here since we were babies," she said. "He's never bitten anyone."
I didn't believe her. One story felt bigger than all those years.
It took till the winter holidays, when Dilnaz and I counted every dog we passed for a week, forty-one dogs and zero bites, before the fear started to shrink.

qa.q: How many dogs did Pankaj and Dilnaz count in a week?
qa.a: They counted forty-one dogs and zero bites.

qa.q: Why did the old brown dog suddenly seem dangerous to Pankaj?
qa.a: The vivid bite story left Pankaj frightened, so one memorable case felt like proof that every dog was dangerous.

qa.q: What helped the fear start to shrink, and why?
qa.a: Counting real dogs for a week with Dilnaz gave Pankaj actual numbers, forty-one dogs and no bites, which showed that bites are rare.

qa.q: How did Dilnaz feel when Pankaj shouted at her to stop stroking the dog?
qa.a: She seemed surprised and a little annoyed, since the dog had been gentle for years.

grounding: It shows a child who hears one scary dog-bite story deciding all dogs are dangerous, as the most memorable case feels like the most common.

It was the Christmas holidays in Lisbon, and Paulo's family planned to drive to his grandparents' village. Paulo, fifteen, didn't want to go.
For weeks his video feed had been full of crash clips: cars sliding on wet roads, pile-ups on motorways, a bus on its side. He had watched dozens. Now every road looked like a disaster waiting.
"We drive there every year," his older brother Mateo said. "Nothing's ever happened."
"You haven't seen the videos."
"I've seen some. They're from all over the world, over years. Of course there are loads."
Paulo shook his head. "It happens all the time. I see it every day."
Mateo held up his own phone. "Because the app keeps showing you what you watch. How many crashes have you actually seen in real life?"
Paulo thought. "None," he admitted, but his stomach still felt tight.

qa.q: How many crashes had Paulo seen in real life?
qa.a: He admitted he had seen none.

qa.q: Why does the road trip feel so dangerous to Paulo?
qa.a: He feels anxious because he has watched dozens of crash clips, so seeing them every day makes crashes feel common in real life.

qa.q: What could help Paulo judge the risk more accurately?
qa.a: He could look at how many trips happen without accidents, and take a break from crash videos so the feed stops filling his head with them.

qa.q: How does Mateo see Paulo's fear?
qa.a: Mateo sees it as a result of the app feeding Paulo more of what he watches, and tries patiently to point out the difference between the feed and real life.

grounding: It shows a teenager who keeps seeing viral crash clips believing travel is far riskier than it is, mistaking how often he sees it for how often it happens.

passage:
In the Onam holidays, Minakshi was home in her small town near Thrissur, and she was frightened of the plane back to college. A dramatic air-crash documentary had been all over her feed, and she had watched it twice. She kept checking the weather on her phone and talking about taking a twenty-hour train instead.
That same evening, she hopped on her cousin Irfan's scooter to go to the temple festival, hair loose, no helmet.
"You're scared of a plane," Irfan said, "but not of this?"
"This is just two kilometres."
"And the road has no lights, and the festival crowd drives like crazy."
"Planes crash, Irfan. You saw the documentary."
"How many scooter accidents have you heard of in this town this year?"
She thought of three, at least. She went quiet. Then she took the spare helmet from the hook without a word.

qa.q: What did Minakshi take from the hook at the end?
qa.a: She took the spare helmet.

qa.q: Why does the plane feel more dangerous than the scooter to Minakshi?
qa.a: She feels frightened of flying because the dramatic documentary is vivid in her mind, while ordinary scooter rides feel familiar and safe even though they carry more everyday risk.

qa.q: What could help Minakshi balance her fears?
qa.a: She could compare how often each kind of accident really happens near her, and always wear a helmet on the scooter since that is a common risk she can reduce.

qa.q: How does Irfan see Minakshi's fears?
qa.a: Irfan finds it strange and worrying that she fears a rare plane crash but rides without a helmet, so he pushes her to think about local accidents.

grounding: It shows a student who fears flying after dramatic coverage while riding a scooter without a helmet, as memorable dangers crowd out common ones.

passage:
I'm Harish, and I became a father in March. Two weeks ago my family chat group exploded. Someone forwarded a message: a gang kidnapping babies in our city, dressed as vegetable sellers. No names, no dates, just capitals and exclamation marks.
My mother stopped letting the maid take my son to the park. My aunt called three times a day. My cousin Farhan said we should put a lock on the gate.
Meanwhile, in our own flat, the balcony railing had a gap wide enough for a toddler, medicines sat on a low shelf, and the geyser wire hung loose. Nobody had noticed those for months.
I asked Farhan, "What do the actual numbers say? How many kidnappings in our city this year?" He didn't know. I checked the police website. The rumour wasn't there.
So I spent Sunday fixing the balcony gap and moving the medicines up high. My mother watched, and slowly, she stopped forwarding the messages.

qa.q: What did Harish fix on Sunday?
qa.a: He fixed the balcony gap and moved the medicines up high.

qa.q: How did Harish feel watching the family panic over the forwarded message?
qa.a: He felt uneasy and doubtful, noticing the fear was about a vague rumour while real risks at home went unnoticed.

qa.q: What did Harish do to check the risk, and why is it sensible?
qa.a: He asked what the actual numbers say and checked the police website, then spent his effort on everyday risks at home, like the balcony gap and low medicine shelf.

qa.q: How might Harish's mother feel after watching him fix the flat?
qa.a: She may feel calmer and a bit sheepish, seeing that the dangers at home mattered more than the rumour, which is why she stopped forwarding messages.

grounding: It shows a new father noticing relatives panic over a kidnapping rumour while ignoring everyday risks at home, and asking what the actual numbers say.

In the waiting room of the community health centre, Manjula sat with her neighbour Uma, both waiting for routine check-ups. On the television above them, a news anchor was talking fast about a woman in another state who had been bitten by a snake in her bathroom.
Uma clutched her bag. "That's it. I'm not using the outside bathroom at night any more."
Manjula felt her own skin prickle. The story was vivid: the dark tiles, the coil in the corner. Then she stopped herself. "Wait. How often does that actually happen?"
"It's on the news!"
"That's why it's on the news. Because it's rare." She took out her phone and found the district health page. Snakebites happened, mostly in fields during the monsoon, and very rarely indoors in town.
"So I'll keep a torch and look before I step in," Manjula said. "But I won't stop living."
Uma loosened her grip on the bag, just a little.

qa.q: What was the news story about?
qa.a: It was about a woman in another state bitten by a snake in her bathroom.

qa.q: How did Manjula feel when she first heard the story, and what did she do about it?
qa.a: She felt a prickle of fear at the vivid details, but she paused and asked how often it really happens before changing anything.

qa.q: Why was checking the district health page a wise step?
qa.a: It gave her reliable figures showing the danger was rare indoors in town, so she chose a sensible precaution, a torch, instead of changing her life out of fear.

qa.q: How might Uma feel after hearing Manjula's findings?
qa.a: Uma seems a little calmer, loosening her grip on the bag, though she is still somewhat shaken by the news.

grounding: It shows a person pausing when a vivid news story frightens her, asking how often it really happens and checking reliable figures before changing her habits.

passage:
On the first day after the summer holidays, the Class 4 room smelled of new books and rain. The teacher, Vandana ma'am, said there would be a quick maths quiz in pairs.
Farhan looked around. There was Kunal, quiet, thin, with thick glasses, reading a comic in the corner. And there was Bunty, the loud boy who drummed on the desk and laughed at everything.
Farhan grabbed Kunal's arm. "You're with me." He was sure the boy with glasses was the topper. Bunty got paired with Ritu.
The quiz started. Kunal stared at the questions and whispered, "I'm bad at maths." Across the room, Bunty was scribbling answers and cheering. Bunty and Ritu won.
Farhan sat there, stunned. "But he looks so... noisy."
Vandana ma'am, collecting the sheets, smiled. "Looks don't do sums, Farhan."

qa.q: Who won the maths quiz?
qa.a: Bunty and Ritu won the quiz.

qa.q: Why was Farhan so sure Kunal would be the topper?
qa.a: Farhan felt confident because Kunal was quiet and wore thick glasses, so he looked like a topper, and that look felt like proof.

qa.q: What could Farhan do next time before choosing a partner?
qa.a: He could ask classmates about their real strengths or remember past results, instead of judging by how someone looks or acts.

qa.q: How might Kunal feel being picked because of his glasses?
qa.a: Kunal might feel pressured and embarrassed, knowing he isn't good at maths and that Farhan expected him to be.

grounding: It shows a child assuming the quiet boy with glasses must be the topper and the loud boy must be weak, as appearance stands in for real evidence.

passage:
"The new girl is definitely a nerd," Sonali whispered to Aparna during the Holi-week sports trials. "Look at her: glasses, long plait, carrying three library books. She'll sit on the bench."
"And him?" Aparna nodded at the boy with the loud laugh and the torn sneakers.
"Trouble. Those types always are. He'll get detention by Friday."
The coach blew the whistle for the hundred metres. The new girl put her books down, tightened her plait and flew. She crossed the line three metres ahead of everyone.
Sonali's mouth fell open. "What?"
"And the loud boy," Aparna said, reading the notice board, "is the school chess captain. He's been for two years."
"But he looks like—"
"Like what?"
Sonali closed her mouth. She had been so sure. It had felt like knowing.

qa.q: How far ahead did the new girl finish the hundred metres?
qa.a: She crossed the line three metres ahead of everyone.

qa.q: Why did Sonali feel so sure about the new girl and the loud boy?
qa.a: She felt certain because they matched types in her head, glasses and books for a nerd, loud laugh and torn sneakers for trouble, and that match felt like knowing.

qa.q: What could Sonali try the next time she meets someone new?
qa.a: She could notice her first guess, treat it as a guess, and wait to see what the person actually does before deciding.

qa.q: How does Aparna see Sonali's guesses?
qa.a: Aparna seems quietly doubtful and a little amused, gently pointing out the chess captain notice to show Sonali was wrong.

grounding: It shows a teenager judging who is sporty or trouble from looks and manner and being surprised when reality disagrees, as the match to a type felt like proof.

The college tech fest was during Diwali week, and the student team had only ten days to build their app demo. Arohi had to choose a project lead between two teammates.
Rishabh spoke beautifully. In the first meeting he talked about "vision" and "disrupting campus life" with his hands moving, and everyone nodded. Shankar barely spoke. He sat at the back with a notebook and asked one question: "Who's testing the login?"
Arohi picked Rishabh. He sounded like a leader.
By day six, the demo didn't work. Rishabh had made three more slide decks and no code plan. Shankar, meanwhile, had quietly fixed the login, written a testing checklist and messaged everyone their tasks.
On day nine, with the power going off in the hostel, it was Shankar who organised a laptop rotation so the build finished on time.
Arohi watched him at two in the morning, calm, ticking off the checklist, and felt her stomach drop. She had mistaken the voice for the work.

qa.q: Who organised the laptop rotation on day nine?
qa.a: Shankar organised the laptop rotation.

qa.q: How did Arohi feel watching Shankar at two in the morning?
qa.a: She felt a sinking regret, realising she had chosen Rishabh for his confident speaking rather than for reliable work.

qa.q: What could Arohi do differently when choosing a lead next time?
qa.a: She could look at what each person has actually done, like past projects or task plans, rather than how fluently they speak in meetings.

qa.q: How might Shankar feel after doing the lead's work without the title?
qa.a: Shankar might feel tired and a little overlooked, though also proud that the demo finished on time.

grounding: It shows a student choosing a fluent, confident speaker to lead a project and overlooking a quieter, more reliable teammate, mistaking style for competence.

passage:
I'm Baljeet, and last month I sat on my first interview panel as a new manager. By the fourth candidate, I noticed something uncomfortable.
My two senior colleagues kept lighting up at candidates who looked like our star analyst from last year: same college, same crisp way of talking, even the same kind of watch. "Very much like Vikram," one said, and gave top marks. A candidate named Vidya, who had solved the case study best, got middling scores. "Not quite our type," the other colleague said.
I checked my own notes and realised I'd been doing it too, at least a little.
So after the round, I suggested we try structured scoring: the same four questions for everyone, each marked against a clear rubric, before any discussion. My colleagues grumbled, but agreed to try.
When we re-scored with the rubric, Vidya came first. We hired her. Two months on, she is the best analyst on the team.

qa.q: Who solved the case study best?
qa.a: Vidya had solved the case study best.

qa.q: How did Baljeet feel when noticing the panel's pattern?
qa.a: Baljeet felt uncomfortable, especially on realising the same pull had shaped Baljeet's own notes a little.

qa.q: What did Baljeet propose, and why does it help?
qa.a: Structured scoring, the same questions with a clear rubric before discussion, so candidates are judged on actual evidence instead of resemblance to past successes.

qa.q: How might Vidya have been affected if the panel hadn't re-scored?
qa.a: Vidya, the strongest candidate, would likely have been passed over for not being "our type", and the team would have lost its best analyst.

grounding: It shows a manager noticing a panel favouring candidates who resemble past successes and proposing structured scoring so people are judged on evidence.
